config.title: Forms & Validation

intro.title: Forms & Validation
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple user registration form with real-time validation. You'll learn how to manage form state using React hooks, validate user input as they type, and display helpful error messages. The core concepts include handling form events, implementing validation logic, and providing user feedback. You'll use TypeScript to define types for your form data and React's useState and useEffect hooks to manage state and side effects. By the end, you'll have a functional form that ensures data is correctly entered before submission.
intro.usecase: Forms with validation are essential in nearly every interactive web application. You'll implement them when building user registration forms, checkout flows in e-commerce sites, and contact forms on business websites. These patterns ensure users provide correctly formatted email addresses, passwords that meet security requirements, and properly structured payment information. As a developer, you'll frequently add validation to prevent data corruption and improve user experience by providing immediate feedback when inputs don't meet requirements.

objectives: Construct a controlled form component using React state and TypeScript interfaces.
Implement real-time validation logic for form inputs using event handlers.
Render dynamic validation feedback messages based on user input.
Configure form submission to process validated data and reset the form state.
Integrate multiple form controls (text, email, password) with unified validation rules.
Manipulate form state to conditionally enable or disable the submit button.
Apply TypeScript types to ensure type safety for form values and error states.

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports for React and useState are added to the file.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the import statement. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main Form component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Form that returns a JSX element. Use TypeScript to define the component.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function. Remember to return JSX (like a <div> or <form>) from the component.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the Form component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A Form component is defined and ready to be used.
successCriteria: The Form component is defined as a functional component that returns JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the Form component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure the component is named 'Form' and returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've created a functional component named Form that returns JSX.

steps.title: Define the form state interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named FormState with name, email, and password fields, all typed as strings.
steps.hint: Create an interface with three properties: name, email, and password. Each should have the type string.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a FormState interface that types the form data structure.
successCriteria: The FormState interface is defined with name, email, and password properties, all typed as strings.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You have an interface, but it's missing some fields or incorrect types. Ensure name, email, and password are all strings.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface is not defined or doesn't match the required structure. Define FormState with name, email, and password as strings.

steps.title: Initialize form state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside your Form component, initialize the form state using useState with empty strings for name, email, and password fields.
steps.hint: Use the FormState interface you defined earlier as the generic type for useState. Initialize with an object containing empty string values for each field.
steps.expectedOutcome: The form state is properly initialized with TypeScript typing and empty string values for all three fields.
successCriteria: useState is called with the FormState type and initialized with an object containing name, email, and password properties set to empty strings.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the FormState interface as the type for useState and initializing all three fields with empty strings.
steps.feedbackWrong: The form state initialization is incomplete or incorrect. Remember to use useState with the FormState type and provide initial values for name, email, and password as empty strings.

steps.title: Define the handleChange function
steps.instruction: Inside the Form component, define a function named handleChange that takes a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> as its parameter and updates the form state based on the input's name attribute.
steps.hint: Use the event parameter to access the target input's name and value. Then call setFormState with a function that returns a new state object, spreading the previous state and updating only the property that matches the input name.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a handleChange function that properly updates the form state when called with an input change event.
successCriteria: The handleChange function is defined with a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> parameter and updates the form state using setFormState, correctly handling the input name and value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a handleChange function, but check the parameter type or the state update logic. Make sure you're using the input's name to update the correct property in the state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleChange function is missing or incorrectly defined. Remember to define a function that takes a change event, extracts name and value from event.target, and updates the form state accordingly.

steps.title: Define the handleSubmit function
steps.instruction: Inside your Form component, define a function named handleSubmit that takes a React.FormEvent parameter and prevents the default form submission behavior.
steps.hint: Create a function that accepts an event parameter of type React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement> and calls event.preventDefault() inside.
steps.expectedOutcome: The handleSubmit function is defined with proper TypeScript typing and prevents default form submission.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function accepts the event parameter and calls preventDefault().
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleSubmit function needs to be defined with proper TypeScript typing and prevent default form submission.

steps.title: Add the form element and onSubmit handler
steps.instruction: In the return statement of your Form component, replace the current return value with a <form> element that has an onSubmit attribute wired to your handleSubmit function.
steps.hint: The form element should wrap around where your input fields will go later. Remember to pass the event handler function directly to onSubmit.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a form element that will trigger the submit handler when the form is submitted.
successCriteria: The return statement contains a <form> element
The form element has an onSubmit attribute set to handleSubmit
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've both added the <form> element AND connected the onSubmit handler to handleSubmit.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've replaced the return value with a <form> element and properly connected the onSubmit handler.

steps.title: Add the name input field
steps.instruction: Inside the form element, add a text input field for the name. Set its value to formState.name and wire its onChange event to the handleChange function.
steps.hint: Use an <input> element with type='text', value={formState.name}, and onChange={handleChange}. Remember to give it a name attribute matching the property in your state.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: controlled input for a username
<input type='text' name='username' value={username} onChange={handleInputChange} />
steps.expectedOutcome: The form will have a text input for the name, which updates the formState.name when typed into.
successCriteria: An <input> element exists inside the form
The input's value is bound to formState.name
The input's onChange is set to handleChange
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your input has all required attributes: type='text', name='name', value={formState.name}, and onChange={handleChange}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The name input isn't properly set up. Check that you've added an <input> element with the correct attributes inside the form.

steps.title: Add the email input field
steps.instruction: Inside your form, add an email input field with the name attribute set to 'email', value bound to formState.email, and onChange wired to the handleChange function.
steps.hint: Add an <input> element with type='email', name='email', value={formState.email}, and onChange={handleChange}.
steps.expectedOutcome: The form will have an email input field that updates the formState.email value when typed into.
successCriteria: An email input field with type='email', name='email', value={formState.email}, and onChange={handleChange} is added to the form.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an email input, but make sure it has all required attributes: type='email', name='email', value={formState.email}, and onChange={handleChange}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The email input field is missing or incomplete. Add an <input> element with type='email', name='email', value={formState.email}, and onChange={handleChange}.

steps.title: Add the password input field
steps.instruction: Inside the form element, add a password input field with name='password', type='password', value={formState.password}, and onChange={handleChange}.
steps.hint: Add an <input> element with the attributes name, type, value, and onChange. The name should match the password property in your formState interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: The form will include a password input field that updates the formState.password value when typed into.
successCriteria: An <input> element with name='password', type='password', value={formState.password}, and onChange={handleChange} is added inside the form.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added an input, but check that all required attributes (name, type, value, onChange) are correctly set.
steps.feedbackWrong: The password input field is missing or incomplete. Ensure you add an <input> with the correct attributes inside the form.

steps.title: Add the submit button
steps.instruction: Inside the form element, add a submit button with the text 'Submit'.
steps.hint: Use the <button> element with type='submit' attribute.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a submit button to a form
<button type="submit">Submit Form</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The form will have a submit button that triggers the handleSubmit function when clicked.
successCriteria: A <button> element with type='submit' and text 'Submit' is added inside the form.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but check that it has type='submit' and the correct text.
steps.feedbackWrong: The submit button is missing or incorrect. Add a <button type="submit">Submit</button> inside the form.

steps.title: Add basic validation feedback
steps.instruction: Add conditional rendering inside the form to display validation messages when name, email, or password fields are empty.
steps.hint:
You can use the logical AND (&&) operator to conditionally render a paragraph element when a field value is empty. For example: {formState.name === '' &&

Name is required

}
steps.expectedOutcome: The form will display validation messages below each input field when that field is empty, providing immediate feedback to the user.
successCriteria: Conditional rendering is implemented for all three fields using logical AND (&&) operator to show validation messages when fields are empty.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some validation messages, but make sure all three fields (name, email, password) have conditional rendering for empty values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The validation feedback isn't working as expected. Make sure you're using conditional rendering with the logical AND operator to show messages when formState values are empty strings.
